text:
The maker of Marlboro once promised to quit cigarettes.

They bought full pages in British newspapers: “Our New Year’s resolution — we’re trying to give up cigarettes.”

To put it mildly, they didn’t keep their word.

They started “quitting” early: in 2014, a cigarette you can’t light appeared in Nagoya, Japan, and Milan, Italy.

The tobacco is warmed by a heater, at half the temperature of a flame: your jacket doesn’t smell, there’s no ash, and you can take a puff right in the car.

This is IQOS, and when comedians raved about it on a popular Japanese TV show in 2016, IQOS sold out everywhere.

No fire — so, no harm?

A year later, Swiss scientists captured this “vapor” and found the same toxins as in smoke. Lower levels of most, even higher of one — and eighty-four percent of a cigarette’s nicotine.

They even titled their paper “Smoke by Any Other Name.”

In 2020, the US regulator allowed IQOS to say it contains fewer harmful chemicals — but it still won’t let them say “less harm.”

Remember R.J. Reynolds — the ones who, in 1973, were looking for ways to hook teenagers?

Their own fire-free cigarettes never caught on: one, with a carbon tip, burned through more than three hundred million dollars.

But their old patents survived: in 2021, the US International Trade Commission ruled that IQOS infringed them — and kicked it out of America.

And the promise to quit? In 2024, IQOS had thirty-two million users — and the company sold six hundred seventeen billion cigarettes, more than the year before.

They quit exactly the way you do.

Can you guess what they came back to America with?
